name: Aisha Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at a zinc and lead mine, about nine hundred metres down. The loader's what we call an LHD, load, haul, dump, it's low and long so it fits in the tunnels, and I muck out the ore after they've fired a blast and take it to the ore pass. We go down in the cage at quarter to seven, and the first job is always checking the ground and the gas readings with the shift boss. I like that it's never quite the same twice, every heading's a bit different, but the heat and the dust get into you, and by Thursday my shoulders are like rocks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the shift boss. Who else do you work closely with down there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the health and safety rep for our crew, so I'm the one people come to when a ventilation fan's not doing its job. My offsider is Luka, a young bloke, twenty-four, who reminds me of my brother. And on day shift two of the loaders are now driven by remote from a room on the surface, so sometimes I'm in the tunnel with a machine that's being driven by someone drinking coffee up top. I've done two sessions on that remote set-up myself, it's not bad once you get used to the delay on the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, the remote loaders already showed us what's useful and what's not, and that hasn't changed. At the union meeting I'd say we dodged a bullet, but let's not get lazy about it. Online I'd probably share some article about it and say the money should've gone into ventilation instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I do, which honestly I'm fine with. The remote loaders are going to grow either way, but slowly, and I already know how to use them. So my job's about as safe as a mining job ever is, which isn't very, but no worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd keep my two remote sessions current and maybe ask for a third so I'm on the list when they add more machines. I'd keep putting a hundred a fortnight into the savings like we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like hearing the storm went the other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a mining job is never very safe. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean the price of zinc. When it drops, they cut a level, and that's happened twice in my time here. AI or no AI, that's the thing that actually keeps me up some nights, and nobody in a suit in the city can fix that either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luka in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get his remote ticket anyway. He's young, and even if AI goes nowhere, the remote stuff is creeping in. It's like seatbelts, they come in slowly and then one day everyone's got one.

S0.say: I'd say we dodged a bullet but shouldn't get lazy about it. Online I'd say the money should have gone into ventilation instead.
S0.think: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'm fine with that. The remote loaders will grow slowly either way and I already know how to use them, so my job is no less safe than now.
S0.do: Keeps her remote loader sessions current and asks for a third so she's on the list when more machines arrive. Keeps saving about a hundred a fortnight as now.
S0.feel: Calm, like hearing the storm went the other way.
S0.quote: It's like seatbelts, they come in slowly and then one day everyone's got one.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is grounded: her main worry in the calm picture is the zinc price, not AI. She already has a foot in remote operations and sees it as normal change. As a safety rep, she frames even this picture in terms of ventilation and conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a strong union and decent rules, because change is fine if workers share in it. At the meeting I'd say every machine that goes remote should come with a training place for the person who used to drive it. And I'd say it's actually safer to have fewer people under the ground, I won't pretend it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right, but plenty of my crew wouldn't be. I've got a head start on the remote stuff. The bit that bothers me is that the surface room needs maybe one person for every three machines, so the maths doesn't work for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the remote room straight away, this month, not wait to be asked. I'd push in the safety committee for a proper training plan with dates, and get the union to put it in the agreement. At home we'd keep the savings going, maybe bump it to one fifty a fortnight, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for others and fairly steady for me. And a bit guilty about that, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rocco, mostly. He's fifty-eight, he's been on loaders since before I was born, and he can't read the screen without his glasses, which he never brings. If they pick three out of nine for the room, I'm in and he's out, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Noor, she's twelve, that Mum might be driving from upstairs soon and she'd think that's hilarious. She'd say, so you're playing video games for work. And I'd say, sort of, except the game weighs fifteen tonnes.

S1.say: I'd say this is why we need a strong union and decent rules, because change is fine if workers share in it. Every machine that goes remote should come with a training place, and fewer people underground is genuinely safer.
S1.think: I'd probably be all right because I've got a head start on remote work, but plenty of my crew wouldn't. The surface room needs maybe one person for three machines, so the maths doesn't work for everyone.
S1.do: Puts her hand up for the remote room this month and pushes the safety committee and union for a dated training plan in the agreement. Raises household savings to about one fifty a fortnight.
S1.feel: Uneasy for her crew, steady for herself, and a little guilty about the difference.
S1.quote: If they pick three out of nine for the room, I'm in and he's out, and I'd hate that.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha sees herself as likely to win in this picture and is openly uncomfortable about it. She holds two views at once: fewer people underground is safer, and fewer jobs hurts people she cares about. Her action is quick and practical, but she wraps it in collective rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs the government to act like it's an emergency, because it is. Pay people, guarantee incomes, and slow the companies down if they can't do it fairly. I'd be at every rally I could get to, with the kids if they'd come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is the remote room doesn't save me here. If the AI can drive the loader, it doesn't need me upstairs watching it. My two remote sessions suddenly look like a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sit down with Karim and look at the numbers, we've got about four months saved, and his nursing job is probably the safest thing in our house. We'd stop the extra payments on the car and keep all the cash. I'd go to the union and push for an income guarantee campaign, and I'd write to our local member, which I've done once before about the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry underneath it. The kind where you can't sleep and you lie there doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change things for you, compared with a longer run-up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no retraining that's worth anything, because by the time I finished a course, the course would be out of date. With a longer run-up I could at least move into something with people in it. With two years all I can do is hold on to cash and hope the government's quicker than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Karim's job is the safest in the house. How would that feel, living on his pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've done it before, when I had my knee done and was off for four months. It was tight, we ate a lot of lentils, but we were fine. What I didn't like was feeling useless, and this would be that, but without an end date.

S2.say: I'd say the government should treat this as an emergency: pay people, guarantee incomes and slow companies down if they can't do it fairly. I'd go to every rally I could.
S2.think: The remote room doesn't save me here, because an AI that drives the loader doesn't need me upstairs watching. My remote training suddenly looks like a joke.
S2.do: Reviews the household budget with her partner, stops extra car payments and keeps the roughly four months of savings as cash. Pushes the union to campaign for an income guarantee and writes to the local member of parliament.
S2.feel: Frightened, with anger underneath, and lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: With two years all I can do is hold on to cash and hope the government's quicker than the robots.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture cancels the advantage Aisha felt in the slower one, and she says so plainly. She draws on a real past experience of living on her partner's pay. Her answers stay organised even when she's frightened: budget, union, letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse this time. I'd want the union, the council and the company in one room making a plan for this town by the end of the year. I'd say it online too, and I'd tag our member so she can't pretend she missed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to change direction once, but not twice. I think I'd have to pick something now that people will still want a person for in 2031. For me that's probably safety training, teaching people, or something in health like Karim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into the safety training certificate this year, it's about six months part time, and the company sometimes pays for it. I'd keep the remote work as my day job while I study. And we'd get the savings from four months to six by skipping our holiday to Karim's parents for one year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Five years is short but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why safety training rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already do half of it as the rep, and when things go wrong people want a person who's been in the tunnel. Even if the robots are doing the mining, someone's got to teach the inspectors and the kids coming through what it was like. Maybe that's wishful, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd skip the holiday to Karim's parents. How would that go down at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. His mum would be on the phone within a day. But Karim's practical, he'd see the numbers and he'd agree, and we'd do a video call on Sundays instead. The kids would be more upset about missing the beach than missing their grandma, which tells you something.

S3.say: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse. I'd want the union, council and company in one room making a plan for the town within a year.
S3.think: Five years is enough to change direction once but not twice, so I'd need to pick something people will still want a person for. Safety training, teaching or health seem most likely.
S3.do: Starts a part-time safety training certificate this year, ideally company-paid, while keeping remote work as her day job. Skips one family holiday to lift savings from four months to six.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can work with.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to change direction once, but not twice.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Aisha moves from defence to a single, deliberate change of direction built on her role as safety rep. She is honest that the plan may be wishful. She still pulls collective players into it, which is typical of her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if we waste it. Every mining town should have a plan for what comes after, paid for by the companies that made money here. I'd say that loudly and often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fifty-three, and that's not a bad age to be a trainer or an inspector. Ten years gives me time to finish a course and get some years in before the end point. But I'd still be worried about the bigger question, which is what everyone does when the robots do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the safety certificate, but at a normal pace, and maybe go on to a full diploma. I'd talk to Noor about her subjects and push science, because she likes it and it might keep doors open. I'd get on the town's transition committee if they had one, and if they didn't I'd help start it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More settled than the faster ones. Still a low worry humming, like the fans underground, you stop hearing it but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone would still have the bigger question. What do you mean for your town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots run the mine and the mine still makes money, who gets it? Right now the wages are what keeps the shops open. If that money goes to shareholders overseas, the main street dies, and no amount of retraining fixes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time that you couldn't do in the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be able to do it properly instead of in a panic. And I'd have time to try something and change my mind, which you can't do in five. Karim says I always need two goes at things, and he's right.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it and a disaster if we waste it. Every mining town needs a plan paid for by the companies that made money there.
S4.think: At fifty-three I could be a trainer or inspector, and ten years gives me time to finish a course and get some years in. The bigger worry is what everyone does when robots do everything.
S4.do: Starts the safety certificate at a normal pace and may go on to a diploma. Encourages her daughter towards science and joins or helps start a town transition committee.
S4.feel: More settled, with a low background worry humming like the fans underground.
S4.quote: Still a low worry humming, like the fans underground, you stop hearing it but it's there.
S4.fieldNote: Aisha feels personally more secure with ten years but stays anxious about her town's money once wages disappear. She thinks in systems: who gets the profit if robots run the mine. She values the chance to try and change her mind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is an income guarantee that kicks in automatically, so nobody's begging, and paid training that's real, with a job at the end. And for the town, some of the mine's money staying here instead of flying out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the women. There's about six of us on site, and we fought pretty hard to get in. It'd be a strange thing if the robots took the job just when the place finally had room for us.

headlineQuote: It'd be a strange thing if the robots took the job just when the place finally had room for us.
portrait: Aisha Moreau is a 43-year-old underground loader operator at a zinc and lead mine, the safety rep for her crew, married to a nurse, with two kids and about four months of savings. She already does some remote driving from the surface and sees slow change as normal. In the steady picture she expects to come out ahead and feels guilty for older colleagues, but full AGI cancels that head start. With more warning she'd pick one change of direction, safety training, while pushing her union and town for a shared plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years leaves no time for retraining worth anything.
whatWouldHelp: An automatic income guarantee, real paid training with a job at the end, and some of the mine's money staying in the town.
